info.bio:
Ministry es una banda de metal industrial que estuvo activa durante los años 80, 90 y 2000. Fue una de las bandas pioneras dentro del subgénero de industrial metal. En 1992 editaron Psalm 69 que fue disco de platino y llegó a estar dentro de los top 30. Fueron pioneros en mezclar música dance con un poco de punk, guitarras metaleras y una voz distorsionada.

scenes.name: Metal industrial y post-industrial
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Uno de los logros clave de finales de los ochenta: la fusión de música industrial con hard rock y heavy metal, iniciada por los suizos Young Gods (samples de guitarras metálicas) y KMFDM. Chicago la completa: Ministry de Al Jourgensen (The Land Of Rape And Honey, «Jesus Built My Hot Rod»), Revolting Cocks, Pigface de Martin Atkins y, de ahí, Nine Inch Nails de Trent Reznor, que cambia el destino del industrial (Pretty Hate Machine, The Downward Spiral). El post-industrial: Neurosis, Steel Pole Bath Tub, Cop Shoot Cop, Missing Foundation, Pain Teens, Godflesh de Justin Broadrick, y los proyectos de Jello Biafra (Lard, Tumor Circus).

scenes.name: Industrial, EBM y The Final Cut
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: En 1989-1990 quien no escuchaba techno escuchaba industrial: Nitzer Ebb, Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly y los belgas Front 242 (Front by Front, 1988), con Chicago como centro americano (Ministry, Die Warzau, My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult, Wax Trax). Detroit tuvo su escena: Code Industry, el único grupo industrial enteramente afroamericano, y The Final Cut, de Jeff Mills y Tony Srock, banda de apoyo del grupo house True Faith (con Bridgett Grace) en Paragon, cuyo productor Jerry Capaldi acabó enfrentado a sus artistas y sembró desconfianza entre techno negro y blanco. Deep into the Cut (1990, Big Sex/Interfisch) cruzó EBM y techno; la última cita de Mills con ellos fue en el festival Atonal de Berlín. Srock los llevó hacia el rock (Consumed, Nettwerk, 1991).

podcast.title: Transition to Industrial Sound (1986)
podcast.body: After being dropped by his record label and dabbling in goth music (1984-1985), Al Jourgensen restarted his career. In 1986, through Depeche Mode connections, he collaborated with producer Adrian Sherwood. Sherwood's radical remixes (e.g., for Depeche Mode) impressed Jourgensen with their heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops, leading to the industrial-leaning album "Twitch." "But in 1986, through some Depeche Mode connections, he hooked up with producer Adrian Sherwood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Give It Away Remix (1991) – Ministry's Al Jourgensen Used a Stoned Chicken on the Mixing Console
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen was invited by the Red Hot Chili Peppers to produce a remix of "Give It Away" for their *Blood Sugar Sex Magik* album. His reported method: he brought a live chicken into the studio, blew marijuana smoke in its face until the bird was intoxicated, then let the stoned chicken stagger across the mixing desk. Wherever the chicken left a dropping, Jourgensen made an adjustment to the mix. "He brought a chicken into the studio and blew pot smoke in the chicken's face... Where the chicken pooped, Al made an adjustment to the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Al Jorgensen's Backstage Antics (Lollapalooza 1992)
podcast.body: At a stop on the 1992 Lollapalooza tour, Ministry's leader, Al Jorgensen, was observed throwing furniture (table, lamps, couch, chair, carpet) out of his backstage trailer. He then carried a broken bottle of Bushmills whiskey, taking long swigs despite its jagged neck. Jorgensen then enlisted help to re-arrange the discarded furniture on the concrete outside his trailer, creating an impromptu "living room," and attempted to share his broken bottle of whiskey. "The last thing to come out of the trailer was Al Jorgensen, the leader of ministry. And he was carrying this broken bottle of Bush Mills whiskey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grammy Nomination (1992)
podcast.body: Ministry received a Grammy Award nomination in 1992, indicating their increasing recognition and success within the music industry, even though they ultimately lost to Nine Inch Nails. "Ministry was even nominated for a Grammy Award in 1992."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza "Party in a Bottle" Incident (1992)
podcast.body: Backstage at Lollapalooza in 1992, Al Jourgensen forced someone to drink from a bottle of Bushmills whiskey with a broken, jagged neck, threatening physical harm if they refused. It was later revealed that Jourgensen was known to add a "dollop of acid" to his Bushmills, creating what he referred to as a "party in a bottle," though this particular addition fortunately did not occur that day. "I ended up backstage with Al at Lala Paloza in 1992 and he made me drink from a bottle of bush mill whiskey that had dropped on the pavement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
podcast.body: Ministry was one of the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, which was recognized for its "absolutely awesome" lineup, arguably the best in the event's history. "Ministry. One of the bands to perform in the legendary 1992 Lala Pulusa Festival, arguably the best lineup in the history of that event."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza Peak (1992)
podcast.body: Ministry was at the forefront of industrial music from 1988 onwards, reaching a peak in 1992 when they were the second-highest billed act on the Lollapalooza tour. "Alan Durgensen and Ministry have been at the forefront, peaking in 1992 when they were second from the top on the Lola Palusatour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Matrix Soundtrack Contribution (1999)
podcast.body: Ministry was featured on the first *Matrix* soundtrack, released in 1999. The album was characterized by "really cool heavy stuff," including contributions from other heavy acts like Marilyn Manson, The Prodigy, Rammstein, and Rage Against the Machine. "It was some really cool heavy stuff, Marilyn Manson, Ministry of the Prodigy, Ramstein, Rage Against the Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 2010 Ulcer Rupture and Cardiac Arrest
podcast.body: In 2010, after experiencing prolonged vomiting of blood, Al Jourgensen collapsed and was hospitalized, where he went into cardiac arrest multiple times. Doctors discovered he had a ruptured ulcer, one of 13 scattered throughout his stomach and intestines, with one ulcer positioned over an artery. When that ulcer ruptured, it caused the artery to rupture as well, nearly killing him. "In 2010, he finally collapsed and was rushed to hospital where he went into cardiac arrest several times. Eventually, it was determined that Al was suffering from a ruptured ulcer, and when they opened him up, they found 13 ulcers scattered throughout his stomach and intestines. One of them was perched over an artery. Once that ulcer ruptured, so did the artery, and that's what nearly killed him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acknowledged Influence of Public Image Limited
podcast.body: Ministry is one of the bands cited as having acknowledged the significant importance of Public Image Limited. "Nine-inch nails, massive attack, manic street preachers, ministry, primal scream, they all acknowledged the importance of public image limited."

podcast.title: Al Jourgensen's Alias (Hypo Luxa)
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen used the alias Hypo Luxa when producing Nine Inch Nails' cover of "Get Down Make Love." "If you look at the credits, you'll see that it was produced by someone named Hypo Luxa, which is actually El Jorgonson of Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Al Jourgensen's Backstage Antics at Lollapalooza '92
podcast.body: At the Canadian stop of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival in Barrie, north of Toronto, Ministry's leader Al Jourgensen engaged in notorious backstage behavior. This included throwing various pieces of furniture out of his trailer, drinking from a broken bottle of Bushmills whiskey, and then coercing an observer to help him arrange the discarded furniture into a makeshift "living room" on the concrete. "The last thing to come out of the trailer was Al Jorgensen, the leader of ministry and he was carrying this broken bottle of Bush Mills whiskey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Al Jourgensen's Early Addiction and Leary Association
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen's substance abuse began remarkably early, starting smoking at age 10 and consuming a pack a day by 15. He later became a heavy user of cocaine and heroin. Notably, he lived with LSD advocate Timothy Leary for two years, during which Jourgensen claims he served as Leary's "human guinea pig," a role he cannot fully define. "He started smoking at 10 and was doing a pack of day by the time he was 15."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Appearance on Sweet 75 Album
podcast.body: Members of Ministry contributed to Sweet 75's self-titled debut album in 1997. "featured appearances by Peter Buck of R.E.M., members of ministry"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Associated with Wax Trax
podcast.body: Ministry, fronted by Al Jourgensen, was one of the bands associated with Wax Trax of Chicago, a specialist indie label for heavy music that appeared around 1990. "This was the home of Ministry Front II IV II, Front Line Assembly and Dozens More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Assorted Controversial Actions
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen has a long history of controversial and confrontational behaviors, including stealing drugs from Courtney Love, physically assaulting R. Kelly for an action that distressed Jourgensen's daughter, and attacking Metallica with vegetables. He also insisted that Limp Bizkit frontman Fred Durst wear nothing but a cowboy hat during a vocal session he produced, blew up Ministry's tour bus with a large firework purchased from a homeless person, and was ejected from the Grammy Awards for screaming at Beyoncé. "Al Jorgensen stole drugs from Courtney Love. He punched out our kelly for doing something that freaked out his daughter. He attacked Metallica with some vegetables."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bar Fight While Sober
podcast.body: Despite being clean, sober, and having lost most of his liver, Al Jourgensen still attracts trouble. In one incident at a bar, admiring bikers repeatedly bought him shots. His refusal to drink them, due to his sobriety, insulted the bikers, which then led to a fight breaking out. "He was in a bar once where a bunch of admiring bikers kept buying him shots. But because Al was straight and sober, not to mention without most of his liver, he didn't drink him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Front 242 Members
podcast.body: Several members of Front 242 actively assisted Ministry during their transition, appearing on what were described as "groundbreaking records" in the mid-80s, solidifying the cross-pollination between the two bands. "Several members of Front II-IV II actually helped in Ministries' transition by appearing on those groundbreaking records of the mid-80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Declared Influence
podcast.body: Ministry is among a partial list of artists and bands who have publicly stated that they have been influenced by Joy Division in some way. "You too, arcade fire, smashing pumpkins, nine inch nails, to pesh mode, sisters of mercy, ministry, chain addiction, the smiths, Bjork, Jesus and Marychain, Moby, primal scream, the Charlotains, Interpol, editors, white lies, Frans Ferdinand. I could go on, but I think you get the point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Deepening into Alt-Rock
podcast.body: Exploring the 1990s alternative music landscape often led listeners to discover heavier or more experimental acts like Ministry, signifying a move into more intense and diverse sounds within the genre.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Depeche Mode "Give It Away" Remix with Stoned Chicken
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen was commissioned to create a new mix of the Red Hot Chili Peppers' hit song "Give It Away" from their album "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," working with John Frusciante in the studio. According to the anecdote, Jourgensen brought a chicken into the studio, allowed it to wander across the mixing board, blew pot smoke into its face to induce a stoned state, and then made adjustments to the song's mix based on where the chicken "pooped" on the board. "The story is that Al brought a chicken with him and let the chicken wander all over the mixing board."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drum Samples Used by ZZ Top in Late 1980s
podcast.body: Ministry's drum sounds were sampled and utilized by ZZ Top on some of their late 1980s records. These samples were triggered and credited to ZZ Top's drummer, Frank Beard, indicating an early instance of inter-band sample usage. "Not physical drums, but samples taken from Ministry Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Technopop Career
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen (referred to as "Alan") initially fronted a Technopop band from Chicago that toured with Depeche Mode and Culture Club. Despite record company expectations and playing the "corporate game" for a while, his record label eventually dropped him. "Alan was in a Tectopop band from Chicago that had spent some time touring with both Depeche Mode and Culture Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Epiphany at Front 242 Show
podcast.body: Legend holds that Al Jourgensen experienced an epiphany at a Front 242 show in Chicago, which revealed to him "the error of his meek, techno pop ways" and prompted his band's transition into a harder industrial style. "But legend has it that it was at a Front II-IV II show in Chicago that Alan Durgensen had as epiphany, of sorts, the one that showed him the error of his meek, techno pop ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Example of Diverse Alternative Music
podcast.body: Ministry was cited as an example of "heavy industrial music" that fell under the "alternative" classification. This underscores the broad scope of the "alternative" genre, which could include various heavy and experimental sounds. "Heavy industrial music from skinny pop and ministry was alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goth Aesthetic Retention
podcast.body: Even after crossing the line into industrial music, Ministry maintained Goth characteristics, particularly in their fashion and stage props. "And even after they crossed that line, ministry maintained Goth properties, especially in terms of fashion and stage props."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Industrial Breakthrough (Early 90s)
podcast.body: Ministry was one of the industrial-minded groups that "broke through from the parallel universe" at the beginning of the 1990s, some even arriving before Grunge became dominant. Their success contributed to industrial music's brief moment in the mainstream. "Out of Chicago came ministry, which began having gold and platinum-selling albums in 1989."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Industrial Hip Hop Dabbling
podcast.body: Ministry is mentioned among artists who "dabbled" in elements of Industrial Hip Hop, particularly through beat-heavy keyboard and drum machine music in the mid-1980s. "Ministry came at DM and 9-inch nails dabbled in this, especially with various 12-inch remixes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
podcast.body: Ministry was a significant influence on Trent Reznor's musical direction, particularly their "rage and fury." This inspiration contributed to Trent's shift from his earlier techno-pop influences towards the harder, more sinister industrial sound that defined Nine Inch Nails. "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Influential Alternative Band
podcast.body: Ministry is recognized as one of the groups that emerged from the changes in the new music scene initiated by bands like the Ramones and Sex Pistols, contributing to the alternative genre. "And now thanks to them and many others, we have groups like the Chili Peppers and Pearl Jam, R.E.N., the Ministry, smashing pumpkins, Jesus Jones, and thousands more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influential Alternative Band
podcast.body: Ministry was mentioned as one of the groups that emerged and contributed to the evolving "new music scene," following pioneers like the Ramones and Sex Pistols. "we have groups like the Chili Peppers and Pearl Jam, R.E.M., the Ministry, smashing pumpkins, Jesus Jones and thousands more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspired by Skinny Puppy
podcast.body: Ministry is explicitly listed as an artist who was inspired and influenced by the Canadian industrial band Skinny Puppy. "Here's a short list of artists who say they were inspired and influenced by Skinny Puppy, Ministry, Nine-inch Nails, Maryland Manson, the Prodigy, Ramstein, Filter, Corn, Lincoln Park, Evan Essence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kubrick's "AI" Film Project and Jourgensen's Antics
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen was reportedly approached by director Stanley Kubrick to compose music for a new film titled "AI." Despite Kubrick's admiration for Ministry, Jourgensen repeatedly insisted that "AI" actually stood for "anal intruder" and suggested the project should instead be a porn film. Following Kubrick's death, Steven Spielberg had to intervene to "clean things up" and resolve the situation caused by Jourgensen's disruptive behavior regarding the film. "He somehow got mixed up with director Stanley Kubrick, who wanted him to write music for a new film. He was going to call AI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Life-Threatening Health Crises
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen experienced a near-fatal overdose on New Year's Eve 1992, during which he was clinically dead for a period. He contracted Hepatitis C from a contaminated needle and suffered a toe infection from excessive injecting, which led to gangrene and required amputation. He also almost lost an arm after being bitten by a spider. In addition to heroin and cocaine, he extensively used crack, ketamine, and meth. His ultimate decision to stop drug use came after his gastrointestinal tract exploded, resulting in the loss of 65% of his blood and another clinical death experience. "Al ended up with Hepp C from a contaminated needle. After injecting a toe so much, it turned gangrous and he had to have it amputated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Maintaining Presence in Grunge Era
podcast.body: Despite the overwhelming focus on guitar music during the grunge era, acts like Ministry still maintained a primary focus, indicating that not all alternative music was completely squeezed out.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ministry/Butthole Surfers Collaboration Recording
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen recorded a song with Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers, a process complicated by Haynes being extremely high throughout the entire session. Haynes was only capable of screaming through a megaphone and eventually fell off his stool. Jourgensen dedicated two weeks to meticulously editing all of Haynes's vocal tracks to create usable material for the song. "Gibby was so high the entire time that the only thing he could do is scream stuff through a megaphone and then he fell off his stool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Evolution
podcast.body: Ministry began as a lightweight technopop band, transitioned through a distinct, though brief (a couple of years), Goth stage, and then evolved into one of the heaviest industrial bands. "They started out as a distinctly lightweight technopop band and went through a distinct Goth stage before becoming one of the heaviest industrial bands around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New Music Scene Development (Early 90s Perspective)
podcast.body: Ministry was mentioned as one of the groups that emerged and contributed to the evolving "new music scene," following pioneers like the Ramones and Sex Pistols. "we have groups like the Chili Peppers and Pearl Jam, R.E.M., the Ministry, smashing pumpkins, Jesus Jones and thousands more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pivot to Goth
podcast.body: Alan Jorgensen pivoted his band Ministry from a light technopop sound to something very gothic, exemplified by their goth anthem "Everyday Is Halloween." "Alan Jorgensen pivoted his band ministry from being a light technopop band to something very Gothic, releasing every day as Halloween, a Goth anthem."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Popularity of Industrial Music (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: Ministry was cited as a prominent group driving the popularity of Industrial music in the early and mid-1990s. "Industrial music was hot thanks to groups like Nine Inge Nails and Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Era Presence
podcast.body: Ministry was an act that retained a place on alternative playlists during a period when guitar music, particularly grunge, became the dominant sound, showing that industrial and other genres still found an audience. "Yes, there were still acts like the Beastie Boys and the Chili Peppers and Ministry and Alannis Moore said, but the primary focus remained guitar music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Era Presence
podcast.body: Despite the overwhelming focus on guitar music during the grunge era, acts like Ministry still maintained a primary focus, indicating that not all alternative music was completely squeezed out.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prominence in Alt Rock Dance Clubs (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: By the early 1990s, Ministry was among the artists whose music was regularly played in hundreds of clubs dedicated to the Alt Rock dance scene. These clubs accommodated people dancing to a wide range of alternative music. "hundreds of clubs devoting several nights of week, if not all nights of the week, to accommodating people who wanted to dance to everything from Nirvana and Nine-inch Nails to Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: Side Project 1000 Homo DJs
podcast.body: Ministry's Al Jourgensen initiated a side project called 1000 Homo DJs to release some of Ministry's outtakes. This project utilized fake names for all contributing members, including Jourgensen (Lux/Buck Satan), his songwriting partner Paul Barker (Pan/Officer Aggro), and drummer William Rieflin (We Willy Riefer), and even featured uncredited vocals from Trent Reznor. "He started a goofy side project called 1000 Home Old DJs as a way of releasing some ministry outtakes while keeping things separate from his main band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: If That Is Your REAL Name

podcast.title: Sympathy for Trent Reznor
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen was very sympathetic to Trent Reznor's contract situation with TVT Records, which led to their collaboration on the 1000 Homo DJs project. "Al Jorrenson was very sympathetic to Trent's situation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

concerts.title: Lollapalooza Festival (1992)
concerts.body: Ministry performed on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival. The mosh pit during their set was vividly described as "what hell must look like from above," and the festival was notable for a bizarre backstage incident involving their leader, Al Jourgensen. "Ministry, one of the bands to perform in the legendary 1992 Lala Pallosa Festival, arguably the best lineup in the history of that event."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell, and Al Jourgensen – Bile Beer Drinking Contest at Lollapalooza 1992
xref.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell (Soundgarden), and Al Jourgensen (Ministry) entered a competition for who could drink the most bile beer. Cornell tried and retched; Jourgensen managed it two days in a row; Eddie was there every single night and claimed to have drunk two quarts more than anyone. When asked why, Eddie said: "Just looking for attention." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Supergroup Lineup and Origins (1994-2001)
xref.body: Tapeworm was conceived as a side project during Nine Inch Nails' "The Downward Spiral" sessions in 1994, intended as a collaborative effort for Danny Lohner and Charlie Clouser. It evolved to include a star-studded lineup: Trent Reznor, Maynard James Keenan (Tool), producer Alan Molder, Atticus Ross, Phil Anselmo and Rex Brown (Pantera), Page Hamilton (Helmet), Toni Halliday (Curve), Tommy Victor (Ministry), and drummer Josh Freese, with at least an album's worth of material recorded by 2001. "If you're Trent Rezner, Danny Loaner and Charlie Closer from his live band, Maynard James Keenan from Tool, producer Alan Molder and Atticus Ross. I mean, wow, awesome, right? The idea for tapeworm went as far back as the sessions for the downward spiral in 1994. Tapeworm was designed as something to which Danny and Charlie could contribute as equals. This idea evolved into something pretty cool. Maynard was brought in, Phil and Salmo from Pantera, Paige Hamilton from Helmut, Tony Haliday from a cool band called Curve, Tommy Victor from Ministry, drummer Josh Freeze. And then in 2001, Alan Molder apparently helped record at least an album's worth of stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Project History (1995-2004)
xref.body: This project was created in 1995 and involved Trent Reznor, Atticus Ross, and a variety of friends, continuing off and on for nine years. Despite the collaboration, nothing was ever officially released. "I already mentioned the tapeworm project, which was created in 1995 and included a lot of different friends. They were continued off and on for nine years, but nothing was ever released."

xref.title: Broadway Musical Character
xref.body: John Bechtel is the touring keyboard player for Ministry and has also played with Fear Factory, Killing Joke, and Prong. xref.title: Day Jobs and Punk Discovery
xref.body: After finding a house with Deborah (eventually settling at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, where he had a room for his poetry), Ian initially worked in a record store in downtown Manchester, where he discovered punk rock. He later secured more stable employment within the British Civil Service, moving between several parts of the bureaucracy, such as the Ministry of Defense and an unemployment office. "He got a day job in a record store at downtown Manchester, which is where he discovered punk rock."

xref.title: Early Career as "Alan"
xref.body: Before Ministry, Al Jourgensen (referred to as "Alan") was in a Technopop band from Chicago that toured with Depeche Mode and Culture Club. He initially tried to play the "corporate game" for his record company before being dropped. "Alan was in a Tectopop band from Chicago that had spent some time touring with both Depeche Mode and Culture Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Example of Diverse Alternative Music
xref.body: Skinny Puppy was listed as an example of "heavy industrial music" that was classified as "alternative." This highlights the extensive stylistic diversity that the "alternative" label covered, ranging from industrial sounds to other forms of non-mainstream rock. "Heavy industrial music from skinny pop and ministry was alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Industrial Breakthrough
xref.body: Nine Inch Nails, led by Trent Reznor, emerged as an even bigger industrial group than Ministry, winning a Grammy Award in 1992. Their success, including regular rotation on Alt Rock stations, represented a significant breakthrough for industrial music from the fringes into the mainstream in the early 90s. "But they lost out to an even bigger industrial group, Trent Rezner and Nine-inch Nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Industrial Hip Hop Dabbling
xref.body: KMFDM is cited as an artist who explored elements of Industrial Hip Hop, especially through beat-heavy keyboard and drum machine music originating in the mid-1980s. "Ministry came at DM and 9-inch nails dabbled in this, especially with various 12-inch remixes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Industrial Hip Hop Dabbling with Remixes
xref.body: Nine Inch Nails "dabbled" in sounds related to Industrial Hip Hop, particularly through their various 12-inch remixes, which fused hip hop elements into their beat-heavy electronic music. "Ministry came at DM and 9-inch nails dabbled in this, especially with various 12-inch remixes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Ministry's Al Jourgensen
xref.body: A Front 242 show in Chicago is famously cited as the location where Al Jourgensen of Ministry had an epiphany, causing him to re-evaluate his "meek, techno pop ways" and leading to Ministry's transition into a harder industrial sound. "But legend has it that it was at a Front II-IV II show in Chicago that Alan Durgensen had as epiphany, of sorts, the one that showed him the error of his meek, techno pop ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Other Artists
xref.body: Their distinctive approach to electronics, heavy beats, and samples had a profound influence on many artists, including Nine Inch Nails and Ministry. "Their approach to electronics and heavy beats and samples influenced everyone from nine inch nails to ministry and beyond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
xref.body: Front 242 was a key influence on Trent Reznor, specifically their "rage and fury." This inspiration helped guide Trent's evolving sound towards the more aggressive, industrial style adopted by Nine Inch Nails. "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
xref.body: Skinny Puppy was a profound influence on Trent Reznor, particularly their sound's "rage and fury." They were instrumental in his shift away from techno-pop and towards the more aggressive, industrial direction that characterized early Nine Inch Nails material, directly inspiring his first song in this new style, "Down In It." "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

xref.title: Inquest into Stage Collapse Findings
xref.body: A lengthy and complex inquest was held following the Downsview Park tragedy, involving the Ontario Ministry of Labor, promoter Live Nation, and stage builder Optex. The initial case ended in a mistrial, requiring a restart. The inquest ultimately determined that the stage roof's design was outdated and unable to support 76,000 pounds of equipment, leading to 28 recommendations from the jury, and declaring Scott Johnson's death accidental. "In the aftermath, a long and confusing inquest was held involving the Ontario Ministry of Labor, Live Nation, the promoter, and Optex, the company commissioned to build the stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Marcus Mumford's Career Path Change
xref.body: After attending Captain Kick and the Cowboy Ramblers' performance at The Bosens Locker, Marcus Mumford was so impressed that he dropped out of Edinburgh University, where he was expected to follow his parents into the ministry, and committed to music as his vocation. "Marcus was so impressed by what he heard and saw that he dropped out of university and vowed to make music his vocation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ministry's Outtakes Project
xref.body: 1000 Homo DJs served as a "goofy side project" initiated by Al Jourgensen of Ministry to release material, specifically Ministry outtakes, while maintaining a clear separation from the main band. The project involved all contributing members adopting fake names for their credits, including Jourgensen (Lux/Buck Satan), Paul Barker (Pan/Officer Aggro), and William Rieflin (We Willy Riefer), and famously included uncredited vocals from Trent Reznor. "He started a goofy side project called 1000 Home Old DJs as a way of releasing some ministry outtakes while keeping things separate from his main band."

xref.title: Nivek Ogre's Other Bands and Acting Career
xref.body: The other notable member, Nivek Ogre, has participated in various other bands, including Ministry with Al Jourgensen, and has developed an interest in working on low-budget horror films, with "Queen of Blood" being a mentioned example. "The other member of note is Nivik Ogre. He's been in a bunch of other bands, including Ministry with Al Jorgensen, but he really seems to enjoy working in low budget horror films. You might want to look up a movie called Queen of Blood."

xref.title: Popularity of Industrial Music (Mid-90s)
xref.body: Nine Inch Nails was cited as a prominent group driving the popularity of Industrial music in the early and mid-1990s. "Industrial music was hot thanks to groups like Nine Inge Nails and Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Grunge Era Presence
xref.body: Despite the overwhelming focus on guitar music during the grunge era, the Beastie Boys were an act that maintained a presence on alternative playlists, indicating some diversity still existed alongside the dominant grunge sound. "Yes, there were still acts like the Beastie Boys and the Chili Peppers and Ministry and Alannis Moore said, but the primary focus remained guitar music."

xref.title: Profound Influence on Multiple Genres
xref.body: PiL had a significant impact on several music genres, including industrial and punk funk. Bands such as Nine Inch Nails, Massive Attack, Manic Street Preachers, Ministry, and Primal Scream have acknowledged PiL's importance. "He hung out with some funk musicians, and eventually pulled together a band that ended up having a profound effect on several genres of music, including industrial and punk funk."

xref.title: Prominence in Alt Rock Dance Clubs (Early 1990s)
xref.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers were part of the musical landscape of Alt Rock dance clubs in the early 1990s. Their music was featured alongside other alternative artists in clubs that catered to a dance-oriented audience. "hundreds of clubs devoting several nights of week, if not all nights of the week, to accommodating people who wanted to dance to everything from Nirvana and Nine-inch Nails to Ministry and the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Radical Remixes for Depeche Mode
xref.body: Adrian Sherwood created "pretty radical remixes" for Depeche Mode songs like "People Are People" and "Master and Servant," characterized by heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. These remixes were highly influential, particularly on Al Jourgensen of Ministry. "Adrian had created some pretty radical remixes for Depeche Mode, most notably for people are people and master and servant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Running Crazed Management
xref.body: In addition to her label work, Marsha Zazula also operated Crazed Management. Her management roster included notable artists such as Ace Frehley of Kiss, Ministry, Testament, and King's X, demonstrating her significant role in artist development and career guidance. "She also ran crazed management, which included clients like Ace Freely of Kiss, Ministry, Testament, and King's X."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Secret Recording as 1000 Homo DJs
xref.body: During his contract dispute with TVT Records, Trent Reznor secretly recorded vocals on a cover of Black Sabbath's "Supernaut" for the Ministry spin-off band 1000 Homo DJs. There is a dispute whether his vocals actually appear on most versions; only versions specifically labeled "Trent Rezner Vocal Version" feature his voice, otherwise it's Al Jourgensen's voice with distortion. "The result was that Trent had to record secretly and under fake names. One such recording was a ministry spin-off band called 1000 homo DJs."

xref.title: Toured with Ministry's Early Band
xref.body: Culture Club toured with Alan Jourgensen's early Technopop band from Chicago, providing an early association for the artist who would later become a pioneer of industrial music. "Alan was in a Tectopop band from Chicago that had spent some time touring with both Depeche Mode and Culture Club."

xref.title: Used Ministry Drum Samples on Late 1980s Records
xref.body: ZZ Top incorporated drum samples taken from Ministry records into some of their albums released in the late 1980s. The drum sounds attributed to Frank Beard on these recordings were, in fact, triggered samples originally sourced from Ministry. "those drum sounds from Frank Beard are actually triggered Ministry samples."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Widespread Influence
xref.body: Skinny Puppy is cited as a major inspiration and influence for a long list of prominent artists including Ministry, Nine Inch Nails, Marilyn Manson, The Prodigy, Rammstein, Filter, Korn, Linkin Park, and Evanescence. "Here's a short list of artists who say they were inspired and influenced by Skinny Puppy, Ministry, Nine-inch Nails, Maryland Manson, the Prodigy, Ramstein, Filter, Corn, Lincoln Park, Evan Essence."
